Understanding AIO conceptually is valuable, but implementation requires specific, actionable tactics that demonstrably improve your chances of appearing in AI-generated responses. These seven strategies have proven effective across different content types, industries, and AI platforms. They work because they align with how language models evaluate sources and decide which content to cite when formulating answers.

The first tactic centers on incorporating statistics, numbers, and verifiable proof throughout your content. AI models exhibit a strong preference for factual, data-backed information over general statements or opinions. When a model encounters two sources covering the same topic, one making vague claims and another providing specific numbers with citations, the statistical content almost always wins.

It has been revealed that this doesn't mean stuffing your content with random numbers. It means grounding your claims in specific, verifiable data wherever possible. Instead of writing "Our tool is widely used," you'd write "Our tool has 150,000 monthly active consumers with a 4.7 out of 5 satisfaction rating based on 3,200 reviews." The specificity signals credibility to AI models, which learned during training that precise data indicates reliable sources.

The same principle applies to any factual claim. When discussing market trends, cite specific growth percentages and time periods. When mentioning tech giant performance, include actual revenue figures or user counts. When describing product features, provide concrete specifications rather than abstract descriptions. Each piece of specific data you add increases the likelihood that AI models will view your content as authoritative and citation-worthy.

This approach requires sourcing and maintaining accurate information, which means you can't fabricate numbers or exaggerate metrics. AI models increasingly cross-reference claims across sources, and inconsistencies damage credibility. The data you include must be truthful and, where relevant, attributed to primary sources. But when you consistently provide specific, accurate information, you build a reputation as a reliable source that AI models return to repeatedly.

The second tactic involves active engagement on Reddit, Quora, and similar community forums. This strategy works for a less obvious reason than you might expect. It's not primarily about direct traffic from forum posts, though that can be valuable. It's about creating authentic mentions and discussions of your content across platforms that AI models frequently encounter during training and web searches.

Language models learn from vast datasets that include substantial amounts of community discussion content. Reddit threads, Quora answers, and forum posts represent genuine human conversations about real topics, making them high-value training data. When your content or expertise appears naturally in these discussions, it creates signals that AI models recognize and incorporate into their understanding of what resources exist and who's knowledgeable about specific topics.

Industry observers note that the key word here is "naturally." AI models have learned to recognize and discount obvious spam, self-promotion, and link-dropping. Simply posting your URL in relevant threads won't help and might actually hurt if it generates negative reactions or gets flagged as spam. Instead, you need to participate genuinely in communities where your expertise is relevant, providing real value in discussions and mentioning your content only when it truly addresses someone's question or adds to the conversation.

Industry observers note that this means answering questions thoroughly, sharing insights from your experience, helping solve problems, and building a reputation as a knowledgeable contributor before you ever share links. When you do reference your content, it should be in the context of "I wrote a detailed guide about exactly this problem that covers X, Y, and Z" rather than "Check out my site." The former contributes to the discussion while the latter feels promotional.

Over time, this authentic participation creates a distributed network of references to your expertise and content across platforms that AI models access. These organic mentions, especially when they're accompanied by positive community response, signal that you're a legitimate authority worth citing. The impact accumulates gradually but compounds over months as you build a presence in relevant communities.

It has been revealed that the third tactic focuses on optimizing for natural language queries rather than keyword stuffing. Traditional SEO often encourages optimizing for specific keyword phrases, sometimes at the expense of natural writing. You might structure sentences awkwardly to include exact keyword matches or repeat phrases more often than sounds natural. This approach can work for search engines that match keywords mechanically.

AI models process language differently. They understand semantic meaning and context, not just keyword matching. When people query AI tools, they ask complete questions in conversational language: "What's the best WordPress hosting for SaaS applications?" rather than "WordPress hosting SaaS." Your content needs to answer these natural questions directly and comprehensively to appear in AI responses.

According to recent reports, this means structuring your content around questions your audience actually asks. Include FAQ sections that address common queries in full-sentence question format. Write subheadings as questions rather than just topics. Provide complete answers that someone could understand without additional context. Make your content readable and helpful to humans first, trusting that AI models will recognize and value that quality.

It has been revealed that the practical implementation involves thinking about the conversation your audience wants to have rather than the keywords they might type. What are they trying to accomplish? What confuses them? What decisions are they facing? What objections or concerns do they have? When you address these elements in natural, conversational language, you simultaneously create content that people find valuable and that AI models recognize as comprehensive answers to common questions.

Industry observers note that the fourth tactic requires creating comparison tables and structured data that AI models can easily parse and reference. Language models excel at processing structured information organized in clear, consistent formats. When they encounter well-formatted comparison tables, step-by-step lists, or data organized in predictable structures, they can extract and cite that information more reliably than when similar content appears in dense paragraphs.

This doesn't mean every piece of content should become a table or list. It means that when you're presenting information that naturally fits structured formats—comparisons between options, sequential steps in a process, multiple examples of a concept, sets of tips or recommendations—you should use formatting that makes that structure explicit and easy to process.

It has been revealed that for example, if you're comparing different software tools, create an actual comparison table with columns for features, pricing, pros, and cons rather than describing each tool in paragraph form. If you're explaining a multi-step process, number the steps and use consistent formatting for each. If you're providing examples, use a predictable structure where each example follows the same pattern.

The benefit extends beyond AI optimization. Structured content is easier for human readers to scan and comprehend too. People increasingly skim content rather than reading every word, and clear structure helps them extract key information quickly. When you optimize for both AI processing and human scanning through better structure, you improve the experience for all visitors while increasing AI citation rates.

Implementation requires evaluating your existing content and identifying opportunities to add structure without forcing it artificially. Look for places where you're listing multiple items in prose that would be clearer as bullet points. Find sections comparing options that would benefit from table format. Identify processes that could be broken into numbered steps. These changes often improve content quality while making it more AI-friendly.

Sources indicate that the fifth tactic involves building multi-platform authority by publishing consistent information across different channels. AI models, particularly those with web search capabilities, often cross-reference information across sources to verify accuracy and assess credibility. When they find the same core information presented consistently on your website, in your social media content, in articles you've published elsewhere, and in your responses on community platforms, it signals that you're a legitimate authority on that topic.

This doesn't mean duplicating content identically across platforms, which could create SEO problems and doesn't align with best practices for different mediums. It means maintaining consistent expertise, perspectives, and factual information while adapting the format and style to each platform's norms and audience expectations.

Your core message and expertise should be recognizable across a blog post on your website, a LinkedIn article, a Twitter thread, a YouTube video description, and a guest post on another site. The specific examples might vary, and the depth of coverage will differ based on format constraints, but the fundamental information should align. This consistency reinforces your authority and makes it easier for AI models to identify you as a reliable source on specific topics.

Sources indicate that building this multi-platform presence takes time and consistent effort. You can't create authority across channels overnight, but you can develop a systematic approach to repurposing and adapting your best content for different platforms. Each piece of substantial content you create should have a distribution initiative that gets the core insights in front of audiences across multiple channels over time.

In a recent development, the strategic value compounds as your presence grows. Early on, you might only appear in AI responses when the model happens to encounter your website. As you build presence across platforms, the model has multiple opportunities to encounter your expertise from different angles, increasing the likelihood that it recognizes you as an authority worth citing.

The sixth tactic emphasizes showing fresh patch signals throughout your content. AI models, especially those with real-time web access, demonstrate preference for current information over dated content. When choosing between two sources covering the same topic, with one clearly recent and another older, the fresher content usually gets cited unless there's a compelling reason to reference historical information.

This creates both an opportunity and a maintenance requirement. The opportunity is that regularly updating content can improve AI citation rates even if the core information hasn't changed dramatically. The requirement is that high-performing content needs periodic refreshes to maintain its competitive position as newer articles on the same topics emerge.

Making freshness obvious requires explicit signals that AI models can easily detect. The most straightforward approach is including "Last updated: [Date]" at the top of articles, making it immediately clear that the content reflects current information. This simple addition can significantly impact whether AI models view your content as relevant for queries about current state or recent developments.

Sources indicate that beyond patch dates, freshness signals include referencing recent events, citing current statistics and data, mentioning the current year in context where relevant, and updating examples to reflect current tools and practices. These signals reassure both AI models and human readers that the information hasn't become outdated even if the core topic is relatively stable.

Recent findings suggest that the practical challenge is balancing the benefit of updates against the time investment required. You can't refresh every piece of content constantly, so prioritize based on importance and competitive pressure. Content that generates significant traffic or ranks well in AI responses deserves regular attention to maintain those positions. Content about rapidly changing topics needs more frequent updates than evergreen material. Content facing new competition from recently published articles needs refreshing to remain competitive.

Sources indicate that implementing a content refresh schedule helps manage this systematically. Rather than updating randomly when you remember, establish a process where high-value content gets reviewed quarterly or semi-annually. During these reviews, upgrade statistics, add recent examples, remove dated references, and add the new update date. This structured approach ensures your most crucial content remains fresh without requiring constant attention to every article.

Sources indicate that the seventh tactic involves implementing JSON-LD structured data markup on your web pages. This technical optimization helps AI models understand your content's structure and purpose by providing machine-readable information about what your page contains, what type of content it is, and how different elements relate to each other.

Structured data uses a standardized format called Schema.org vocabulary implemented through JSON-LD script tags. These tags don't affect how your content appears to human visitors, but they provide clear signals to automated systems parsing your pages, including AI models determining whether your content answers specific queries.

Common structured data types relevant for most content include Article (marking blog posts and articles), HowTo (for step-by-step guides), FAQ (for question-and-answer sections), Person (for author bios), Organization (for company information), and Product (for product pages). Implementing appropriate schema markup for your content type helps AI models categorize and understand your content more accurately.

The technical implementation requires adding JSON-LD scripts to your page HTML, typically in the header section. Many content management systems, including WordPress, offer plugins that generate this markup automatically based on your content, eliminating the need for manual coding. For custom implementations, Schema.org provides documentation and examples for each data type.

While structured data implementation requires more technical knowledge than the other tactics, its value extends beyond AIO. Search engines like Google also use structured data to create enhanced search results like rich snippets, knowledge panels, and featured answers. This means the optimization work benefits both traditional SEO and AI visibility simultaneously.

The cumulative effect of implementing all seven tactics is substantial. Each strategy individually improves your chances of appearing in AI responses, but they work synergistically when combined. Content that includes specific statistics, appears in community discussions, answers natural language questions directly, presents information in structured formats, exists consistently across platforms, reveals clear freshness signals, and implements proper schema markup sends multiple reinforcing signals that AI models recognize and value.

In a recent development, understanding individual tactics is vital, but sustainable success requires integrating AIO into your overall content strategy rather than treating it as a separate, occasional activity. This means developing systematic approaches that maintain and improve your AI visibility over time without requiring constant manual intervention.

It has been revealed that the foundation of any sustainable strategy is creating content with AIO in mind from the beginning rather than retrofitting optimization after publication. This doesn't mean abandoning your audience's needs to serve AI algorithms—it means recognizing that content optimized for AI models is typically also better for human readers because both value clarity, structure, accuracy, and comprehensiveness.

When planning newly introduced content, start by identifying the questions your target audience asks AI models about your topic. These questions form the backbone of your content structure. If you're writing about project management tools, for example, you'd want to address questions like "What's the best project management software for small teams?", "How much do project management tools typically cost?", and "What features should I look for in project management software?" Each of these questions likely deserves a dedicated section with a clear, direct answer.

Your content outline should reflect these natural queries in your subheadings and section structure. This organizational approach simultaneously improves readability for humans scanning your content and makes it easier for AI models to identify which sections answer specific questions. When someone asks an AI about project management tool features, a model searching your content can quickly locate and cite the relevant section because you've structured it logically around that question.

The next consideration is information density and specificity. AI models favor content that provides concrete, actionable information over vague generalizations or superficial coverage. This means investing in depth rather than breadth for your most crucial topics. A comprehensive 3,000-word guide that thoroughly addresses a topic will typically perform better in AI citations than ten shallow 300-word articles that skim the surface.

Industry observers note that this depth requirement influences content strategy decisions about volume versus quality. Rather than publishing something latest every day with minimal research, you might publish twice weekly but ensure each piece provides genuine value with proper research, specific examples, and comprehensive coverage. The quality-focused approach generates better long-term results both for human audiences and AI visibility.

Recent findings suggest that maintenance and updates become critical components of sustainable strategy. AI models accessing the web in real-time naturally favor fresh content, so static articles gradually lose visibility even if they were initially successful. Building systematic content review and refresh processes prevents this decay and maintains your competitive position.

In a recent development, A practical maintenance schedule might review your top-performing content quarterly, your mid-tier content semi-annually, and your long-tail content annually. During these reviews, you update statistics and examples, add upcoming sections covering recent developments, remove or update outdated information, and add a new "last updated" date to signal freshness. This regular maintenance keeps your content competitive and indicates both AI models and human visitors that you're actively maintaining accuracy.

Competitive analysis should inform your ongoing strategy. Monitor which sources AI models cite for queries where you want visibility. Analyze what makes those sources effective—is it their structure? Their level of detail? Their use of data and statistics? Their freshness? Understanding your competition's strengths helps you identify gaps in your own content and opportunities to differentiate through superior quality or unique angles.

Recent findings suggest that this competitive intelligence doesn't mean copying what others do well. It means understanding the bar you need to meet or exceed to compete for AI citations in your niche. If competing content provides basic overviews, offering in-depth analysis gives you an advantage. If competitors focus on theory, adding practical examples and case studies differentiates you. If everyone covers similar points, finding unique angles or addressing overlooked aspects of the topic creates competitive advantage.

Distribution and promotion strategies must extend beyond traditional channels to build the multi-platform presence that signals authority to AI models. This means systematically sharing your expertise across relevant communities, contributing to discussions on forums and social media, publishing on platforms like Medium or LinkedIn in addition to your own site, and building genuine relationships within your niche rather than just broadcasting content.

According to recent reports, the goal isn't maximum reach across every possible platform—that's neither sustainable nor effective. Instead, identify the two or three platforms where your target audience genuinely spends time and where your expertise provides value. Focus your distribution efforts there, building consistent presence and contributing meaningfully over time. This focused approach generates better results than scattered efforts across a dozen platforms.

Collaboration and linking strategy matter differently for AIO than for traditional SEO. While backlinks remain crucial for search engine rankings, AI citation rates appear more influenced by the quality and relevance of the connection than purely by link volume. Being cited by a highly authoritative source in your niche can boost AI visibility even if it provides only one link, while dozens of low-quality directory links might not impact AI citations at all.

This suggests prioritizing genuine partnerships, guest posting on respected sites in your industry, and earning mentions from authoritative sources through excellent work rather than pursuing link-building tactics focused purely on volume. The relationship-based approach to link acquisition aligns well with AIO because it creates the kind of genuine authority signals that AI models recognize and value.

Understanding where AI search is headed helps you prepare for upcoming changes rather than constantly reacting to latest developments. While predicting specific features or timeline is difficult, several clear trends are shaping the evolution of AI-powered discovery.

It has been revealed that the most obvious trend is continued growth in AI search usage. As more people discover tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, and as these tools improve their interfaces and expand capabilities, the percentage of information-seeking behavior flowing through AI models will increase. This doesn't necessarily mean traditional search engines will disappear, but it does mean the traffic pie is being redivided, with AI search claiming an expanding slice.

Industry observers note that this growth trajectory suggests that early adoption advantages in AIO will compound over time. Establishing strong AI visibility now, while competition remains relatively light, positions you favorably as usage explodes and competition intensifies. The content creators building AI authority today will have structural advantages over those who wait until AI search is fully mainstream and optimization becomes more competitive.

Integration between different search modalities is accelerating. Google is bringing AI answers into traditional search results. Bing is integrating ChatGPT-powered features. Upcoming platforms are emerging that combine search, AI chat, and traditional browsing in unified experiences. This convergence means optimization strategies must account for hybrid discovery experiences where users might see both traditional results and AI-generated answers, potentially in the same interface.

The technical sophistication of AI models continues advancing rapidly, with implications for optimization strategies. Future models will better understand nuance, maintain longer context, cross-reference information more effectively, and potentially access real-time data more seamlessly. These improvements might make some current optimization tactics less crucial while creating upcoming opportunities for differentiation.

Recent findings suggest that for example, as models improve at understanding semantic meaning and context, exact keyword matching will matter even less than it does now. Conversely, models might become better at assessing content quality through subtle signals like writing sophistication, logical coherence, and comprehensive coverage. This evolution favors creators focused on genuine quality over those trying to game systems through technical tricks.

Personalization in AI search is emerging as models learn to consider individual user preferences, history, and context when formulating responses. This creates both opportunities and challenges for content visibility. The opportunity is that AI might recommend your content more prominently to owners whose preferences align with your perspective or style. The challenge is that you might become invisible to users whose personalization profile doesn't match, even if your content is objectively relevant to their query.

Adapting to this personalized future likely requires building distinct brand identity and perspective rather than trying to be everything to everyone. If AI models categorize you clearly—as the practical, actionable advice source versus the theoretical deep-dive resource—you'll appear reliably for owners whose preferences match that positioning. Trying to be too generic might result in appearing rarely for anyone as models route users to more distinctive alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that commercial considerations will shape AI search evolution as platforms figure out monetization beyond subscriptions. We're already seeing early experiments with citations including affiliate tracking, sponsored placements in AI responses, and premium content partnerships. The specific implementations will evolve, but the trajectory toward commercial integration seems certain.

For content creators, this commercial evolution might create new opportunities to monetize AI visibility beyond indirect traffic benefits. If platforms begin sharing revenue with cited sources, strong AI visibility could become directly profitable. If sponsored placements become normalized, there might be ways to amplify your organic visibility through paid promotion similar to how PPC complements SEO.

It has been revealed that regulation and AI model behavior around copyrighted content remains in flux, with implications for what content models can reference and how prominently different sources appear. Current legal frameworks are struggling to accommodate AI's information synthesis capabilities, and future regulations might significantly impact how models cite sources, what compensation creators receive, and what controls you have over whether AI systems can reference your content.

According to recent reports, staying informed about these regulatory developments and adjusting strategy accordingly will matter increasingly. The content creators who navigate this evolving landscape successfully will be those who remain flexible and adapt to changes rather than expecting today's rules to persist indefinitely.

Transforming AIO knowledge into actual improved visibility requires systematic implementation rather than sporadic efforts. Here's a practical framework for incorporating these strategies into your content workflow.

Sources indicate that start with an audit of your existing content to identify which pieces should be prioritized for AIO optimization. Not every article deserves equal attention—focus first on content that already performs well in traditional search, addresses notable topics for your audience, or covers queries where you have genuine expertise to offer. These high-potential pieces are most likely to generate meaningful results from optimization efforts.

Industry observers note that during the audit, evaluate each priority article against the seven optimization tactics. Does it include specific statistics and verifiable data? Could you add more? Is the content structured with clear headings that reflect natural language questions? Have you included an FAQ section addressing common queries? Is there a clear "last updated" date? Can you add comparison tables or other structured data? Does schema markup exist and is it appropriate for the content type?

Create a prioritized optimization checklist based on this audit, identifying which pieces need which improvements. Some content might only need a few additions like enhancement dates and FAQ sections, while others might benefit from more substantial restructuring. This systematic approach prevents you from trying to fix everything at once and ensures you tackle the highest-impact improvements first.

Industry observers note that implement changes incrementally, testing as you go rather than making all modifications simultaneously. This allows you to learn which specific changes seem to impact your AI citation rates most significantly. While many factors influence visibility, you might discover that certain tactics work particularly well for your niche or content style, allowing you to prioritize those approaches for future content.

For latest content creation, build AIO considerations into your standard workflow. Before writing, identify the key questions your content will answer and structure your outline around those questions. Initiative to include specific data points and examples during research. Decide what structured elements (tables, step-by-step lists, comparisons) would enhance the content. Add these considerations to whatever content creation process you already use rather than treating AIO as a separate, optional step.

Establish monitoring routines to track your AI visibility over time. Whether you use commercial tracking tools or build your own system, schedule regular reviews of your performance. Monthly checks might suffice initially, though weekly monitoring makes sense if you're actively optimizing and want faster feedback on what's working.

When reviewing tracking data, look for patterns rather than obsessing over individual fluctuations. Is your visibility generally improving, declining, or stable? Which topics show stronger AI citation rates? Where are competitors consistently appearing instead of you? What queries used to show your content but no longer do? These patterns inform where to focus future optimization efforts and what's working well versus what needs adjustment.

Build a distribution schedule that ensures your content reaches the platforms where community discussion happens. Rather than sporadic promotion when you remember, systematically share newly introduced content and participate in relevant discussions on a regular cadence. This might mean dedicating 30 minutes daily to community engagement, or setting aside specific times weekly for distribution activities. The consistent approach yields better results than irregular bursts of activity.

Industry observers note that document what works as you implement and test different approaches. Keep notes on which tactics seem most effective for your content, which platforms drive the most engaged traffic, which topics generate the most AI citations. This knowledge base becomes increasingly valuable over time as you identify patterns specific to your niche and audience that might differ from general best practices.

Industry observers note that consider forming or joining groups of content creators in your niche who are also working on AIO to share insights and results. The field is new enough that collective learning accelerates progress for everyone involved. What you discover about effective tactics in your niche might help others, and their experiences can inform your strategy even if you're in slightly different spaces.

Plan for iterative improvement rather than expecting immediate perfection. AIO is still an emerging practice without definitive best practices etched in stone. You'll make mistakes, try things that don't work, and occasionally optimize for factors that turn out not to matter. This experimentation is part of the learning process. What matters is systematic iteration—trying approaches, measuring results, adjusting based on feedback, and gradually improving your effectiveness over time.

Industry observers note that set realistic timelines for seeing results. Unlike paid advertising where you can generate traffic immediately, organic visibility through either SEO or AIO builds gradually. You might see some quick wins from optimizing high-performing content, but establishing strong overall AI visibility typically takes months of consistent effort. Understand this going in to maintain motivation during the initial period where you're investing effort without dramatic visible results.

The opportunity in AI Optimization exists because most content creators haven't recognized its importance yet. Traditional SEO remains the primary focus, while this emerging traffic channel grows rapidly with relatively light competition. This window won't stay open indefinitely. As more people understand AIO's value, competition will intensify and optimization will become more sophisticated.

According to recent reports, your competitive advantage comes from starting now rather than waiting until AIO is fully mainstream. Begin with these immediate actions that require minimal investment but start building your foundation.

First, test your own AI visibility today. Open ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity and ask questions where your content should logically appear as a relevant source. Be honest in your queries—use the actual questions your audience would ask rather than phrasing things to favor your content. See whether AI models cite you, and if so, how prominently. This reality check indicates you where you stand currently.

Sources indicate that second, identify your top five most vital pieces of content—articles that address core topics for your audience or drive significant traffic currently. These become your initial optimization targets. Don't try to optimize everything at once. Focus on making these five pieces as strong as possible for AI citation.

Third, implement quick wins on those priority pieces. Add "Last updated: [current date]" to each. Create a simple FAQ section addressing three to five common questions related to each article's topic. Add specific statistics or data points if they're at the moment missing. These improvements take hours rather than days but can meaningfully impact AI visibility.

Fourth, set up basic tracking even if you don't build a comprehensive system immediately. Create a simple spreadsheet listing queries where you want visibility. Test those queries weekly in one or two AI platforms and note whether your content appears. This manual tracking takes just 15-30 minutes weekly but provides feedback on whether your optimization efforts are working.

Fifth, join one or two communities where your target audience discusses topics related to your content. You don't need to be everywhere—pick platforms where you can genuinely contribute value and commit to participating regularly. Start by reading and understanding the community culture before posting, then gradually engage in discussions where your expertise adds value.

It has been revealed that the investment required isn't massive. You don't need expensive tools, extensive technical knowledge, or a large team. You need understanding of the principles, systematic implementation of practical tactics, and consistency over time. The same qualities that make someone successful with traditional content creation—providing genuine value, maintaining quality standards, and persisting through the gradual process of building authority—work for AIO as well.

According to recent reports, the difference is timing. Traditional SEO is mature with intense competition and well-established players dominating many niches. AIO is emerging with room for newcomers to establish authority while the landscape is still taking shape. This timing advantage creates opportunities for content creators of all sizes to build significant AI visibility if they act now rather than waiting.

Start today. Audit your content. Implement quick optimizations. Begin tracking your performance. Engage in communities. Build the multi-platform presence that signals authority. Each small step compounds over time into substantial competitive advantage as AI search grows to represent an ever-larger percentage of how people discover information online.

The future of organic visibility includes AI citations alongside traditional search rankings. The question isn't whether to optimize for both—it's whether you'll start while competition is light or wait until fighting for AI visibility becomes as challenging as ranking in traditional search is today.

Industry observers note that choose wisely. The traffic is already flowing. The only question is whether it flows to you or your competitors.

Breaking: Teachback: learning while coding with AI

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after using agents for all sorts of software engineering work, I started noticing that I was retaining less of what I learned.
  • I built teachback with inspiration from a second study on metacognitive scripts.
  • The agent writes code only after I explain why the change is needed and how it connects to other parts of the project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after using agents for all sorts of software engineering work, I started noticing that I was retaining less of what I learned. I wasn't the only one: in How AI Impacts Skill Formation, 52 participants with Python experience learned Trio, an asynchronous programming library they had never used before. The paper reports a 15.4% difference in quiz scores, with the AI group scoring lower, and no statistically significant improvement in task time. Among the AI interaction patterns, Iterative AI Debugging had the lowest quiz score, while AI Delegation finished fastest, with an average score of 39%. That led me to create teachback, a tool to help me retain what I'm learning while working with an agent. I also ran a small experiment to see how it worked for me.

I built teachback with inspiration from a second study on metacognitive scripts. The study explores ways to keep people cognitively active while using AI. One idea I took from it is a gate: the agent asks the user to explain not only what a change does, but why it is needed and how it connects to the rest of the project. In the study, participants who used a gated AI assistant repaired a regression in the next phase of the same session at a rate of 61.5%. That was close to the 69.2% rate for participants who worked without AI, and higher than the 23.1% rate for participants using ungated AI. The task was controlled, and the study cannot separate the effect of the explanation from the extra friction of the gate, but the results encouraged me to try the idea.

I built the skill around three parts:.

In a recent development, gate. The agent writes code only after I explain why the change is needed and how it connects to other parts of the project. Simply restating what the code does isn't enough; if my explanation misses the causal link, the agent asks a follow-up question.

Recent findings suggest that solo or worked examples. I write the parts I already know, and the agent reviews them afterwards. For parts I don't know, the agent gives me a worked example that I can extend. The idea is that familiar parts should be straightforward for me to implement, which helps me retain that knowledge. Ideally, this works even better with a memory system, such as ai-memory, so the agent can tell which parts of the project I already know.

Recall. Staying active during a session matters, but I also want to fill knowledge gaps and remember what I learned later. After each gated piece, teachback uses my answers to check for a knowledge gap and asks whether to add that concept to a review list. It uses the FSRS algorithm to schedule spaced reviews, which an agent hook presents at the start of a later session.

Recent findings suggest that the complete protocol uses all three parts. It also leaves debugging to me: the agent won't read my tracebacks or suggest fixes, though I can ask conceptual questions.

I didn't test the recall feature in this experiment. I added it later, and although spaced repetition has support from other research, I haven't tested teachback's recall feature itself.

I compared using teachback to fix prometheus/client_python issue #1177 with full delegation to fix opentelemetry-python issue #5726. The experiment is documented in the learn repository, which kept its original name after I renamed the tool. Before each fix, I answered the same five questions using only the issue description. Eight days after each fix, I answered them again from memory.

I’ve published my answers, the answer keys, and the blind grading results so you can see what I recalled and how the scores were reached.

In a recent development, with teachback, my score went from 1/5 to 3.5/5, a gain of 2.5 points. With delegation, it stayed at 2.5/5, with no measured gain. The ordering matched my prediction that recall would be better after using teachback, although both after-scores were half a point below what I predicted.

Sources indicate that the bugs weren't equally difficult. The delegated bug was more straightforward. The teachback bug was harder: assumptions in the matter description initially sent me in the wrong direction, and I needed context from the agent to understand the problem. So the score difference is consistent with teachback helping me retain more, but this small comparison cannot show that the method alone caused it.

Using teachback took 86 minutes; full delegation took 11 minutes. That's about 7.8 times as long, compared with my prediction of 3 times as long. I think much of the difference came from the bugs: the delegated one was straightforward, while the teachback bug required knowledge I didn't have, and following the matter description alone pointed me toward the wrong solution. The agent had context that helped me, but teachback required me to explain why each step was needed before passing its gates, then implement the parts I could handle myself. That took time. Since I used each method on a different bug, I can't separate the time spent on the method from the time spent on the bug's difficulty. I expect that cost to be worthwhile for complex or sensitive business logic, where not understanding a change creates real risk.

These results are encouraging for teachback: I recalled more after using it in this comparison. But this was one bug per method, and the bugs differed in difficulty. The numbers describe what happened in this experiment, not a general effect we can expect from the tool.

Industry observers note that this experiment doesn't prove that teachback takes 7.8 times—or even 3 times—as long as full delegation. Those times came from two different bugs, and the difference will vary with the task. It also can't tell us how much of the recall difference came from the method: I tried each approach on only one bug, and those bugs weren't equally difficult. Comparing both methods on the same task would bring another problem: after solving it once, I couldn't erase what I'd learned before trying the other method.

Recent findings suggest that so, the experiment suggests that I recalled more after using teachback, but it doesn't establish how much the skill preserves learning or how much time it adds across tasks. I still think it's worth trying. If you want to avoid knowledge gaps while working with an agent, give it a try, open an matter, and let me know what you think.

#162143. A Handover That Only Works Warm Is Not a Handover

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1103 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

A Handover That Only Works Warm Is Not a Handover

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A handover that only works warm is not a handover.
  • alexshev asked the question in the comments on the recovery piece.
  • Industry observers note that the job was a tiny interval-merge helper for a scheduling side project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A handover that only works warm is not a handover. It is a diary with a to-do list attached. That is the claim, and the test behind it is small enough to describe in full: one folder, one fresh operator who had never seen it, one failing test, and under two minutes from first read to a green suite. Nothing was missing. Nothing had to be guessed. I am going to tell you what was in the folder, because the folder is the whole result.

alexshev asked the question in the comments on the recovery piece. A recovery blueprint should be a durable artifact, not a memory of the last conversation: checkpoints, known-good inputs, pending approvals, and the exact next command, all living where a fresh operator can resume safely. The run he proposed was simple to state and easy to dodge: write the artifact for a real multi-step job, kill the chat, resume cold from the artifact alone with a fresh operator, and report what was missing, what had to be re-derived, and whether the exact next command was actually enough. So I built a small job and handed it to someone cold.

Industry observers note that the job was a tiny interval-merge helper for a scheduling side project. The artifact was three files in one folder. NOTES.md held the spec: merge overlapping intervals, sorted by start, touching intervals merge into one, do not mutate the input, empty in means empty out. It held what was done: the function implemented, four tests written. And it held what was left: one test failing, fix the code not the test, add a test for unsorted input, run the suite and leave it green. It also held the exact command to check the work. intervals.py held the function, with one real bug in it: the merge boundary used greater-than-or-equal, so touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] stayed separate instead of merging into [1,3]. test_intervals.py held four tests, three passing, one failing on exactly that case.

The fresh operator got one thing: the path to the folder. No chat history, no explanation, no hints about where the bug was. It read the notes, ran the suite, found the boundary, changed one character, added the unsorted-input test, and ran the suite again. Five passed, zero failed, in 0.03 seconds of test time. The whole thing, from the handoff to the green suite, took under two minutes. Its report back remarked there was nothing to guess: the spec stated the touching rule explicitly, the failing test matched it, and the fix followed directly. The one judgment call it made on its own was writing the fresh test with two assertions instead of one, covering both the merging and the non-merging unsorted cases.

That is a pass. Here are four problems with it, because a pass on a tiny job is not a pass on the idea.

The job was tiny, and tiny jobs flatter their notes. One bug, one character, one rule. A real multi-step job has steps that depend on each other, state that lives in three places, and a fix that is not visible from the failing test. The notes passed this test because there was almost nothing to get wrong. Scale is the untested part, and it is the part that matters: the notes would have to carry ordering, state locations, and the exact point of no return, and none of that was exercised here.

It has been revealed that I handed the operator the path. That is the half of alexshev's question I did not test, and his follow-up names it directly: for work that can wake someone at 3 AM, he wants the file linked from the on-call surface, because a perfect file is useless if nobody can find it from the alert. My operator never had to find the folder. It was given the address. The finding half, the cold start in the dark, is still untested, and it is the half that fails most often in real life.

The operator was the same kind of worker as the one that wrote the notes. It reads carefully, follows instructions literally, and does not skim. A tired human at 3 AM skims. A human might have missed the touching rule in the spec, or read the failing test as the thing to fix instead of the code. The notes say "fix the code, not the test" in plain words, which helps, but nothing in this run says how the notes survive a reader who does not read them fully.

The fix was one character, and one-character fixes do not test judgement. The operator never had to decide between two plausible fixes, never had to choose what to leave out, never faced a step where the notes were silent. The most useful thing the notes did was state the rule the test depended on. On a job where the rule itself is the argument, the notes would have to carry the reasoning, not just the rule, and that is a harder document to write.

So the claim stands, but narrowly: the artifact survived a cold start, on a small job, with the address handed over. What survived was the spec plus the exact next command plus the failing test as the pointer to the bug. That combination is the part worth stealing. A spec alone leaves the operator guessing where to start. A command alone leaves them guessing what done looks like. A failing test alone leaves them guessing what the rule is. The three together left nothing to guess, and the clock says so: under two minutes, zero questions asked.

According to recent reports, what was missing the last time you resumed something cold? Not the last time you read a handover, the last time you actually picked up work you had never seen, with no one to ask. What did you have to re-derive, and how long did it take before you trusted that you had it right? I want the missing piece, not the success story. The success story here is one folder and two minutes. The missing piece is what the next version of the notes has to carry.

Sources indicate that P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam.

#162136. Oracle November 2026 Critical Security Patch Enhancement: 640 CVEs and Java4Shell

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1233 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Oracle November 2026 Critical Security Patch Enhancement: 640 CVEs and Java4Shell

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Credit: Oracle Corporation / Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain).
  • Sources indicate that oracle's monthly Critical Security Patch Update cadence is only six months old, yet November's release reads more like a full quarterly overhaul.
  • Industry observers note that since launching monthly CSPUs in May 2026 to bridge the gap between larger quarterly Critical Patch Updates (CPUs), Oracle has used the third Tuesday of each month to push high-priority fixes faster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Credit: Oracle Corporation / Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain).

Sources indicate that oracle's monthly Critical Security Patch Update cadence is only six months old, yet November's release reads more like a full quarterly overhaul. On November 17, 2026, Oracle published its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) Advisory, delivering 655 latest security patches across 640 unique CVEs spanning 21 enterprise product families.

Industry observers note that since launching monthly CSPUs in May 2026 to bridge the gap between larger quarterly Critical Patch Updates (CPUs), Oracle has used the third Tuesday of each month to push high-priority fixes faster. According to Tenable's Research Special Operations analysis published on November 17, 62 of this month's 655 patches carry a Critical severity rating, and dozens of flaws across Java SE, Oracle APEX, Oracle REST Data Services, and Fusion Middleware are remotely exploitable over a network without authentication.

We haven't tested this ourselves; this is based on Oracle's official November 2026 CSPU advisory and Tenable's Research Special Operations breakdown.

In a recent development, when a single vendor drops 655 patches on a Tuesday afternoon, treating every product family with equal urgency slows down remediation where attackers actually aim. Breaking down the distribution immediately shows where the highest concentration of unauthenticated network exposure sits.

It has been revealed that oracle Hyperion absorbs the largest share of fixes by a wide margin, accounting for 267 patches (40.8 percent of the entire November CSPU), including 107 vulnerabilities that can be exploited remotely without credentials. Oracle Supply Chain follows with 74 patches (36 unauthenticated remote flaws), while Oracle E-Business Suite and Oracle Fusion Middleware tie at 71 patches each. Notably, 53 of Fusion Middleware's 71 patches are remotely exploitable without authentication.

At the severity level, 62 patches (9.5 percent) are Critical across 57 unique CVEs, 249 patches (38 percent) are High across 245 CVEs, 274 patches (41.8 percent) are Medium across 268 CVEs, and 70 patches are Low across 70 CVEs.

This table summarizes the highest-volume and highest-severity Oracle product families in the November 17, 2026 CSPU based on Oracle's risk matrices and Tenable's tally.

The numbers in the table show why Java SE, APEX, ORDS, and Fusion Middleware deserve front-of-line attention even though Hyperion holds the raw volume record.

Database infrastructure icon representing enterprise SQL and middleware systems.

Credit: Zahra Ibrahem / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Sources indicate that among the 640 CVEs, one vulnerability already carries a nickname security teams will recognize: CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell by researchers. Reported to Oracle by Albert Yang and Quang Luong of Calif.io, the vulnerability lives in the Compiler component of Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK, carrying a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 High.

What makes Java4Shell stand out is not a 9.8 score on paper, but its reach. All 11 vulnerabilities patched in Oracle Java SE this month are remotely exploitable over a network without authentication. Affected releases span virtually every active enterprise Java branch: Java SE 8u511b33, 11.0.33.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, and 27.0.1.0.3, along with GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.0.3 and 21.0.13.0.3.

Tenable notes that deeper technical details on Java4Shell are expected to surface soon, which usually means proof-of-concept analysis and automated scanning signatures follow closely behind. Organizations running internet-facing Java application servers, API gateways, or build runners should inventory JDK versions now rather than waiting for public exploit write-ups to circulate.

In a recent development, even internal microservices deserve a quick check, because compiler-level flaws in shared JVM runtimes often surface inside container base images that developers pull without thinking about underlying patch levels. Updating base JDK images in CI/CD registries early prevents downstream teams from shipping newly built services on top of vulnerable November 2026 runtimes.

While Java4Shell grabs attention, the highest raw CVSS scores in Oracle's November 2026 advisory hit core database and web-tier components:.

Industry observers note that first, Oracle APEX (versions 24.1.22, 24.2.21, 26.1.5, and 26.2.0) and Oracle REST Data Services (ORDS) (versions 24.2.0 through 26.3.0) share CVE-2026-114849, a CVSS 9.8 Critical HTTPS vulnerability remotely exploitable without authentication (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N). APEX picks up a second 9.8 Critical unauthenticated HTTPS flaw in CVE-2026-114850, while ORDS also patches CVE-2026-114856 at 9.6 Critical (network-exploitable without credentials, requiring only user interaction). Because ORDS and APEX frequently sit directly behind corporate reverse proxies or web application firewalls, leaving them unpatched exposes database-backed web apps to high-impact compromise.

It has been revealed that second, Oracle Database Server (versions 19.3 to 19.33, 21.3 to 21.24, and 23.4.0 to 23.26.4) patches three CVSS 9.9 Critical vulnerabilities in Oracle Text and RDBMS: CVE-2026-114819, CVE-2026-114848, and CVE-2026-114822. These require a Create Session privilege over Oracle Net, meaning an authenticated database user or compromised service account can abuse them to cross security boundaries (Scope: Changed) with High confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact.

Third, Oracle Autonomous Health Framework (versions 26.4 to 26.10) receives a CVSS 9.1 Critical fix for CVE-2026-114847 in its developer triaging platform over HTTP, alongside CVE-2026-19445 (8.1 High in Python TLS handling) and CVE-2026-102274 (7.5 High in PyJWT).

IT technician inspecting server racks inside a data center facility.

Oracle's November 2026 advisory also includes an important reminder for teams running automated vulnerability scanners: VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) justifications are embedded directly below product risk matrices.

According to recent reports, for example, Oracle ships third-party library updates for OpenSSL (CVE-2026-72897, CVSS 7.5), Python (CVE-2026-115557, CVSS 7.4), jackson-core (CVE-2026-89425, CVSS 6.5), and Apache HttpClient (CVE-2026-64607, CVSS 4.3) in Database Server. At the same time, Oracle marks several third-party CVEs in Apache MINA SSHD, DBI, jline, and jsoup as non-exploitable in context (vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path or vulnerable_code_cannot_be_controlled_by_adversary). Reviewing those VEX tags prevents engineering teams from burning sprint cycles chasing false positives in software composition analysis reports.

According to recent reports, oracle also explicitly warns customers not to overlook four standalone October 2026 Security Alerts issued ahead of this CSPU: CVE-2026-91403 (October 21), CVE-2026-114820 (October 24), and CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619 (October 25). If your patching pipeline skipped those out-of-band October alerts, fold them into this week's change window alongside the November 17 CSPU.

Sources indicate that in addition, Oracle reminds administrators that protocol entries in its risk matrices cover secure variants automatically. When HTTP is listed as an affected protocol in an Oracle Fusion Middleware, APEX, or ORDS matrix, HTTPS endpoints are affected as well unless Oracle explicitly notes otherwise.

It has been revealed that trying to patch 655 problems simultaneously across ERP, middleware, and database tiers usually stalls change boards. A tiered rollout focuses effort where unauthenticated attackers have the shortest path:.

Recent findings suggest that if your organization still relies on legacy Oracle releases outside Premier Support or Extended Support, remember that Oracle does not test or issue CSPU patches for unsupported branches even when the underlying code remains vulnerable. Use this November cycle to audit end-of-support versions across MySQL 8.0, older WebLogic domains, and unpatched Java runtimes before December 15 arrives.

Oracle's Critical Patch Updates (CPUs) are full quarterly cumulative releases, whereas Critical Security Patch Updates (CSPUs), introduced in May 2026, ship monthly on the third Tuesday to deliver focused, high-priority fixes between quarterly cycles.

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is an 8.1-rated vulnerability in the Compiler component of Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK that can be exploited remotely without authentication.

Oracle Database Server patches three CVSS 9.9 flaws (CVE-2026-114819, CVE-2026-114848, CVE-2026-114822), while Oracle APEX and Oracle REST Data Services patch CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated HTTPS flaws (CVE-2026-114849, CVE-2026-114850).

Turn every PDF on a web page into text for RAG, without writing a crawler

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (322 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that say a site has a "Reports" page with 30 PDFs and you want their text in a vector store.
  • Recent findings suggest that create a free Apify account if you do not have one, open the Actor and put the page that links to the PDFs into Web pages to scan for PDF links.
  • In a recent development, the first dataset row has type: "inventory".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that say a site has a "Reports" page with 30 PDFs and you want their text in a vector store. The slow part is rarely the parsing. It is finding the links, downloading the files and not paying twice for the same file. Here is how I do it with an Apify Actor I built, PDF to Text Extractor.

Recent findings suggest that create a free Apify account if you do not have one, open the Actor and put the page that links to the PDFs into Web pages to scan for PDF links. Leave sameDomainOnly on so you only get the site's own files. Set maxPdfs to 20 for a first look and pick an output format: per_page, document or markdown.

In a recent development, the first dataset row has type: "inventory". found is every PDF link seen on the page, queued is how many this run takes, and links shows the source page and link text of each. It is free. If found is 34 and queued is 20, you know a full run is about 34 PDFs before you pay for it.

Sources indicate that each PDF is one type: "document" row with status, pageCount, wordCount, the text and metadata. Filter on status == "ok" before indexing. A PDF linked from several pages is extracted once; the copies come back as free duplicate rows.

In a recent development, pages with no text layer are listed in needsOcrPages. The Actor does not do OCR, and a scanned-only file is free, so send those to an OCR tool of your choice and keep the rest.

No OCR, no table extraction, and multi-column layouts can interleave. PDFs behind a login are not found. robots.txt is honored by default.

Recent findings suggest that price is $3 per 1,000 PDFs of up to 100 pages. I built this Actor, so take the comparison with that in mind.

#162129. REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2865 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Blogspot ↗ Open Full Page

REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?
  • What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?
  • Recent findings suggest that you use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code? You use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built. Maybe it is a fast search bar, a clever clipboard trick, or a mechanic in an old game. Until recently, finding out meant months of learning disassemblers and reading assembly code. A new open-source project called REA changes that. It has earned more than 430,000 stars on GitHub, and in this guide I will explain what it does, which problems it solves, and how you can start using it today. In this guide The problem with reverse engineering How REA solves it How REA works What REA can analyze Real examples How to get started REA at a glance Using REA responsibly Frequently asked questions The Problem: Reverse Engineering Is Hard Reverse engineering is the practice of studying finished software to understand how it works. It is powerful, but it has never been beginner-friendly. If you have tried it, or even thought about trying it, you have probably run into these obstacles. 1. A steep learning curve Reading assembly code and pseudocode takes a long time to learn. Many curious developers give up before they get their first useful result. 2. Too many tools and no single workflow An Electron app needs one approach. An Android APK needs another. A .NET assembly, a native binary, and a website each have their own tools, file formats, and tricks. 3. Slow, manual investigation Even experts can spend hours following one function through strings, calls, and references just to understand a single small feature. 4. AI answers you cannot verify If you ask a general chatbot how an app works, it may give a confident answer that is simply invented. Without evidence, you cannot tell what is real. 5. Painful setup Connecting analysis tools to an AI agent usually requires custom scripts and configuration, and it is easy to break. The Solution: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) REA is a free, MIT-licensed project that connects your AI agent to professional reverse engineering tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use external tools. In simple terms, REA acts as a bridge between your agent and the software you want to understand. Here is how it answers each problem above. The Problem How REA Solves It Steep learning curve You ask in plain English. Your agent runs the tools and explains the results. Too many tools One MCP server covers native binaries, Electron apps, Android, .NET, websites, and dozens of other formats. Slow and manual The agent traces code, references, and calls for you. Answers you cannot verify Every result includes the evidence and limitations behind it. Painful setup One command registers REA with your agent and backs up your existing configuration. You do not need the app’s source code. You point your agent at the app, ask a question, and REA helps it trace the answer. How REA Works You ask a question. For example, how a feature in a particular app works. The agent calls REA. It uses MCP to inspect the target and trace the relevant code. REA returns findings. These include code, references, and clearly marked unknowns. The agent acts on them. It can explain the behavior, ask follow-up questions, or write and test its own version of the feature. The same workflows are available from the terminal, so you can also script them without an agent. Analysis runs locally on your machine. Your agent receives the tool results, and your AI provider’s own data policy applies to that part. What Can REA Analyze? The range of supported targets is one of REA’s biggest strengths. These are the main groups. Native programs and binaries REA returns pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls, and references. Deep native analysis uses an engine you already have, such as Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or Kuna. It also supports GNU objdump and Rizin for offline inspection. JavaScript and Electron apps This is the easiest place to start, because static JavaScript analysis needs no native engine. REA recovers modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC connections, and native add-on relationships. Android apps and devices REA can inspect APK manifests, classes, decompiled methods, signatures, and resources. Through adb, it can also look at packages, processes, and logs on an emulator or a real phone. Flutter apps and JEB projects are supported too. .NET and managed code For .NET assemblies, REA reads metadata, CIL instructions, and native dependencies without running the program. Websites and network captures REA can inspect page structure, scripts, and network activity using a Chrome-family browser. It can also read saved HAR and Fiddler SAZ files to examine requests, responses, and exposed payloads. Specialist formats The list continues with Go and Rust binaries, GPU code objects, GGUF and safetensors model files, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK archives, PE imports and certificates, ELF notes, Linux kernel modules, WebAssembly, EVM bytecode, SQLite databases, firmware images, packet captures, and PyInstaller executables. Most of these use built-in static inspection, so no extra software is required. Real Examples: What Has REA Done? The project publishes several case studies on its website. DX-Ball sound panning. REA followed a sound call into a helper function and turned incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passed 3,205 test cases against the original x86 code and matched all 63 compiled function bytes. Notion’s clipboard bridge. REA traced how Notion’s Electron app moves clipboard data from the renderer through preload and IPC into the main process, including the rich clipboard format. TH04 bullet patterns. REA recovered the angle calculations of a classic DOS game and compared the rebuilt C++ with the original compiler output. Bonus: build RL environments from a web app REA can record a web app session and turn its API calls into tools an AI agent can use. It then exports a runnable environment for reinforcement learning or for testing how well an agent completes tasks. With a saved HAR file, the command looks like this: rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json You then run the result with AgentEnv and Docker, and add your own tasks and reward checks. How to Get Started With REA You need Node.js and npm. The project lists supported Node versions as 22.x (22.23.4 or newer), 24.x (24.22.1 or newer), or 26.12.1 and above. Step 1: Run the setup command npx rea-agents setup Step 2: Choose your agents and approve the changes Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents. It shows you the proposed changes first and keeps backups of your existing configuration. Step 3: Restart your agent The new MCP server is loaded when the agent starts again. Step 4: Ask your first question Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. Prefer the terminal? You can inspect an extracted Electron app or ASAR file directly: npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json To keep REA installed, run npm install --global rea-agents. REA changes rapidly, so use rea upgrade to stay current. Updating is also the first fix to try if you run into a bug. REA at a Glance What makes it special REA combines the reach of dozens of analysis tools with the convenience of an AI agent. It helps you understand software you do not have source code for, and it backs each conclusion with evidence instead of guesses. The range of supported formats, from native binaries to Electron apps to Android devices, is unusually broad for a free tool. Key features Works through MCP with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents Evidence and limitations attached to every result Local analysis on your own machine A full command-line interface for scripting Support for dozens of file and app types An RL environment builder Guides and case studies on the official website Pricing REA itself: free and open source (MIT license) Commercial engines such as IDA Pro, Hopper, and JEB: you must obtain these legally under their own licenses Ghidra: a free option for native analysis; see the setup guide for details Perfect for Developers, security researchers, students, software preservationists, and anyone who wants to understand how an app works. Using REA Responsibly Use REA only on software you own or are authorized to examine. The project is intended for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you have permission to study. It does not permit cracked tools, stolen license keys, or bypassing license restrictions. Read the project’s disclaimer before you start. Also be careful where you download it from. The project warns that a similar repository name or a copied README does not make a download official. Use only these sources: GitHub: github.com/morluto/rea Website: rea.tools npm package: rea-agents Frequently Asked Questions Do I need Hopper or Ghidra? Only for deep native binary analysis. JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native engine, and setup can install Hopper with your approval. Does REA upload my app? No. Analysis runs locally. Your agent sees the results, and its provider has its own data policy. Which AI agents work with REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers can use it. What should I do if I find a bug? Update first, because a recent release may already include the fix. If the problem continues, open an issue on GitHub with your REA version, the target type, the steps to reproduce, and the error output. Final Thoughts The old problem was simple: understanding software without source code took too much skill, too many tools, and too much time. REA’s answer is just as simple. It gives your AI agent the tools to investigate, and it requires the agent to show its evidence. Whether you want to learn how a favorite feature works, study a classic game, or inspect an Electron app, REA is a strong place to start. Just make sure you use it only on software you are allowed to examine.

Tech Report: Give Canned Baked Beans A Delicious Upgrade With A Drizzle Of This Ingredient (Hint: It's Not Honey)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Molasses might not be the first thing you think of when you consider add-ins, but many homemade recipes call for it, and for good reason.
  • According to recent reports, it is for this reason that molasses is also preferable to honey here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when you need a side to go along with your main dinner entree and you need one fast, it's reassuring to know that shelf-stable, pantry-sitting canned goods have got your back. Included in Food Republic's list of inexpensive canned foods you'll use all the time are beans, and along with the plain black or red varieties (which typically need to be combined with other ingredients to make a reasonable side), you could also reach for scrumptious, creamy baked beans. But while they're totally fine heated up straight from the can, they can certainly benefit from a drizzle of molasses.

Molasses might not be the first thing you think of when you consider add-ins, but many homemade recipes call for it, and for good reason. Made by boiling down sugarcane juice or refining sugar, the rich, thick syrup is slightly smoky and sweet, with robust, burnt caramel notes, making it a perfect match for deepening the flavor of sometimes weak-tasting canned baked beans and bringing them closer to homemade.

According to recent reports, it is for this reason that molasses is also preferable to honey here. Honey is intensely sweet, can taste almost floral at times, and has a delicate flavor, whereas molasses is bolder and has a meatier taste that can make its presence known among the other ingredients in the dish.

It's important to note that there are three main types of molasses: light, dark, and blackstrap, and they each have different flavor profiles. For canned baked beans, you'll likely want to stick with light or dark because blackstrap is intensely bitter (also, light is the sweetest of the three, so if sweetness is important to you, go with that one). If you're heating the beans on the stove, you can start by drizzling in about half a tablespoon of molasses per 28-ounce can, bringing the mixture to a boil, and then simmering for about 10 minutes. If you're baking them, likewise, just stir in the molasses before putting the dish in the oven — it couldn't be simpler.

If you don't have any molasses sitting about, don't panic. There are plenty of other additions that can help upgrade canned baked beans and make them taste less, well, pantry-fied. Take brown sugar, for example — did you know that it's often just white sugar and molasses combined? A little bit will still bring that sweet contrast to balance out the savory flavors and give you a deeper, more complex finish.

According to recent reports, another great option is one you might normally use on your pancakes: maple syrup. You don't want to use the fake stuff that's primarily made of corn syrup and artificial flavors and colors, but rather 100% real Grade A maple syrup for the best flavor. Its sweetness again deliciously contrasts with and enhances the canned baked beans' savoriness, while the maple flavor adds its unique caramelly, toffee-like notes to the dish.

  • Think of Korean cuisine, and a sandwich likely isn't the first thing that comes to mind.
