  • In a recent development, walk into the closest grocery store near you, ask an employee where that cool fun olive oil is, and they'll take you to a (metaphorically) glowing row of funky green squeeze bottles.
  • You'll undoubtedly notice that Graza has some acolytes waiting on the shelves next to its empire of squeeze bottles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In a recent development, walk into the closest grocery store near you, ask an employee where that cool fun olive oil is, and they'll take you to a (metaphorically) glowing row of funky green squeeze bottles. These are, of course, Graza bottles. It's the sensational olive oil brand that rode to fame on the slick, green waves of cute packaging and a quality product. Graza's oil comes primarily from Jaén, Spain. The company commits to a single origin and single varietal mission, so the oil in your newly-acquired bottle comes from a single place and a single type of olive.

You'll undoubtedly notice that Graza has some acolytes waiting on the shelves next to its empire of squeeze bottles. Whether they existed before or after Graza debuted on the scene, each of these unique oils takes after Graza in some way; some are also from Andalusia, while others sport a youthful aesthetic. If you're interested in what's beyond Graza olive oil, we think these alternatives are totally worth trying out.

According to recent reports, hopping onto the green squeeze-bottle trend is O Olive Oil and Vinegar's organic California Extra Virgin Olive Oil. Though do note that the olive oil also comes in glass bottle form, so there's a version for everyone's packaging preferences. Olive oil-heads will enjoy the fruity notes in this oil that evoke Graza's Sizzle product. Squeeze it into a hot pan for a delicately sweet cooking oil, or combine with any of O's extensive line of vinegars in a dressing or marinade so good you'll want to drink it.

Industry observers note that these bottles proudly wear that tantalizing "first cold pressed" label that tingles our wallets, which is the first signal that you're looking at a quality olive oil. Though all extra virgin olive oils are cold pressed and kept below 80 F, first cold pressed means that the olives were only crushed (or processed) once, making for a richer oil with more nutrients. Besides the label, O California Extra Virgin Olive Oil has a really pleasant flavor that'll be a talented supporting player in your culinary ensemble.

Recent findings suggest that A Greek olive oil whose name screams professional, The Chef's Way oil by Iliada is in a squeeze bottle to provide convenient flavor whenever you need it. The Chef's Way is single-variety and pulsing with Mediterranean flavor like almonds and artichokes, which breaks up your regularly scheduled olive oil programming with a nicely acidic interlude.

It may be scary for the olive oil purists to be accosted by an aisle of squeeze bottles when you walk into the store nowadays. But one easy, squeezy afternoon of cooking will change their minds completely with the undeniable convenience. The Chef's Way olive oil comes in several different flavors, including Kalamata PDO Extra Virgin and Premium Greek Extra Virgin, so you can choose whichever variation calls to you the most. Put on your chef whites, nonslip shoes, and backwards hat, because The Chef's Way is coming to transform your home kitchen into one of those casually elegant eateries.

Costco lovers, you're going to appreciate this find. The Kirkland-branded olive oil warrants its own inclusion in this article because of its robust flavor and versatility. Like Graza, Kirkland's best olive oil comes from Spain, the country that beats Italy as the top olive oil producer in the world.

The Kirkland Signature Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil comes in an absurdly large jug, like many other items at Costco, so you'll get an incredible value for your money. It's the perfect olive oil to use in baking to add a strong, but not abrasive, creaminess. For instance, an olive oil cakes would be the perfect vehicle for the Kirkland Signature Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil. Olive oil cake batters tend to eat up a cup or more of oil, which can get really expensive really fast. You can save your fancy olive oil for other pursuits. But don't worry — this olive oil isn't only suited for baking. It can accommodate your shallow frying and vinaigrette needs, as well.

It has been revealed that another Spanish olive oil from Jaén, Oro Bailén has that slick aesthetic appeal of Graza, along with the high-quality taste. While it can be a little pricier than Graza, it offers something Graza does not: A slightly more acidic olive oil for those times when you want a punchier flavor. The brand offers a few different intensities, so you can choose how much punch you want in your olive oil. Along with the punch, you'll find notes of banana that add a ripeness you don't encounter so often with run-of-the-mill olive oils.

Oro Bailén oils comes from Picual olives, harvested very early and milled very quickly to obtain what it instead calls "olive juice," bringing to mind a flavorful and nourishing elixir you'll want to have in your kitchen. Oro Bailén has a forward quality in its flavor: outgoing, fruity, and spicy. Like Graza, which also sells potato chips, Oro Bailén has some intriguing offshoot products, like EVOO pearls and an olive oil jam for when a simple oil isn't enough to put on bread.

Recent findings suggest that featuring sleek labeling that tells you everything you need to know about the brand, Brightland Extra Virgin Olive Oil belongs to the same cool kids club that Graza is presently the ringleader of. Brightland's product line also closely resembles Graza's, offering several different types of oils for different purposes, including a popular pizza oil (which is different from olive oil). Brightland is the kind of olive oil you'll want to casually leave out on your dinner table to impress your guests.

High in polyphenols, which have healthy antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, Brightland feels as attractively carefree as it looks. The brand has also branched out into different varieties and flavors of oil, as mentioned above, in a manner more abstract and artsy than Graza. "Lucid," "Rosette," and "Arise" are some of the olive oil options when it comes to Brightland, signifying lemon, garlic, and basil. These options give you the same carefree star power you can feel when putting down a bottle of Graza on your table.

In a recent development, if Martha Stewart tells you to get some olive oil, you can expect two things: It'll be wicked expensive, and likely delicious. Flamingo Estate's olive oil line is perhaps a more luxurious option than Graza's, but it has a peppery bite thanks to the quick processing that will be reminiscent of Graza's "drizzle" finishing oil. Martha Stewart swears by this $50 bottle, the olives of which come from Ojai, California.

This oil is green, sumptuous, and glossy — you'll want to dip a finger into it. Though it is cosmically destined for a hunk of crusty bread, Flamingo Estate's oil also has a high smoke point, so you can use this verdant gold in the oven or on the stovetop. The look of it is one of its best qualities, so a fresh drizzle will be a beautiful finish to your dishes. It isn't unlike Martha, when you think about it: It's vibrant, tasteful, and one of the fanciest things you could come across in your kitchen.

It has been revealed that kosterina is an award-winning Greek olive oil, and right away you can tell: Its shiny white bottle looks like it was plucked right from the Mediterranean. The olives for this brand are harvested early, so the resulting olive oil is a little more assertive than Graza's Sizzle, but it's just as versatile. This is a single varietal olive oil, made from only Koroneiki olives that are nutrient- and oil-rich. Single varietal oils can have a crisper flavor compared to blends, and Kosterina is as refined as they come.

Buying a metal bottle of Kosterina olive oil — metal, as it helps prevent oxidation and harmful chemicals leaching into the oil from plastic — feels intentional in a similar way to getting one from Graza. It feels a little better for the environment, and it even tastes like it's doing you good. Another way that Graza's changed the home-cooking game: No longer can a home kitchen function with one singular olive oil. Now, you need one for cooking and another one for drizzling. Kosterina follows suit with this idea, offering even more choices for your olive oil-purchasing escapades.

Industry observers note that A wildly popular olive oil, California Olive Ranch feels a little more homey than some of the other brands on this list. But it's just as good as them: The brand is is backed up by glowing reviews from both customers and publications alike. It offers its olive oil in regular pour bottles, squeeze bottles, oil sachets (for all your emergency olive oil purposes), and even spray cans for your baking pan needs. The grassy, cushiony flavor of this oil makes it one of Giada De Laurentiis' top favorite olive oil brands. In terms of an everyday, affordable olive oil that's still comparable to Graza, California Olive Ranch is where it's at.

With California Olive Ranch, you'll find some top-tier qualities you may be looking for in an olive oil: a balanced taste along with an all-purpose use. Its affordability is just the cherry on top for this great olive oil brand you should try if you want a Graza alternative.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Miami‘s nightlife scene in the 1990s informed the saturated colours and metallic accents used by local studio Evan Edward inside this apartment in the oceanside city, illustrating what the studio calls its “high-impact minimalism” approach.
  • Designed for an international family with “personal ties to the city’s storied nightlife era”, the Miami Beach pied-à-terre reflects the hedonistic era that left a distinct stylistic impression.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ori Harpaz.

Miami‘s nightlife scene in the 1990s informed the saturated colours and metallic accents used by local studio Evan Edward inside this apartment in the oceanside city, illustrating what the studio calls its “high-impact minimalism” approach.

Designed for an international family with “personal ties to the city’s storied nightlife era”, the Miami Beach pied-à-terre reflects the hedonistic era that left a distinct stylistic impression.

It has been revealed that “Aesthetically, there was a rawness to the excess and glamour,” Evan Edward co-principal Josh Evan Goldfarb told Dezeen. It was a particularly exciting time for colour and design in general in the city.

“The city was in its early stages of redevelopment – the original art deco glamour and run-down beach patina were a sublime tropical combination.”.

He and co-principal Michael Edward Moirano set about creating interiors that blend contemporary and vintage furniture and decor to reflect “a more seductive side of Miami”.

Sources indicate that in place of a typical South Florida palette of white, beige and turquoise, spaces feature hues of terracotta, burnt orange, burgundy and ochre. These prevalent tones are complemented by flashes of chartreuse, mustard yellow and metallic finishes.

To create a more welcoming space for entertaining, the designers opened the kitchen to the living and dining spaces with the angular island as a central gathering point.

They also connected the foyer to an adjoining unit behind a series of oversized pivot doors.

It has been revealed that “The updated floor strategy completely changed the experience for the clients,” Moirano told Dezeen. “The triangular island is the hub of the space, serving the kitchen and dining banquette area, while also exposing the living area featuring a dramatic view of Biscayne Bay and the Miami skyline.”.

A butter yellow kitchen was paired with richly veined stone countertops that complement the polished-pebble flooring.

The generous island was illuminated by a 1960s five-pendant light feature above, and accompanied by mustard yellow Calligaris bar stools for casual dining and gathering.

Goldfarb was forthcoming about references to personal experiences and spaces.

“One of the references for the kitchen was an artist studio that I visited when growing up in Coconut Grove – the memory is ingrained in my mind’s eye,” said Goldfarb. “It was just so airy – up in the trees, open windows, patina on all surfaces and artwork and materials strewn about.”.

“The sense of colour and mashup of materials – stone, tile, painted – it’s hard to forget,” he added.

Nestled into a corner, a banquette with olive-toned Rubelli velvet upholstery wraps a circular stainless steel table, while a pair of 1970s folding chromed-steel and leather chairs provide additional seating.

An adjustable lamp by Tito Agnoli for Oluce with a custom shade extends from the wall to hang over the table.

The mellow tones of the kitchen were contrasted by the fiery orange-red of the pivoting foyer doors – a hue that reappears in a bold artwork above the bed in the otherwise neutral-toned primary bedroom.

Metallic accents are dialled up in the powder room where a silver metal mosaic clads the walls and metallic zellige tiles cover the floor.

Moirano described it as a “very sexy disco-inspired discovery off the foyer”.

“The result is a small but impactful space that captures the project’s more theatrical influences through materiality rather than overt decoration,” the studio said.

The team describes the project as an example of its “high-impact minimalism, in which architectural restraint provides a framework for distinctive materials, collectible furnishings, and unexpected moments of visual interest.”.

Located on a barrier island along South Florida’s Atlantic Coast, Miami Beach is renowned for its 1920s art deco architecture and more recent influx of luxury hotels.

Another apartment, on the city’s famous Ocean Drive, was renovated by MW Works to include tropical hardwood and sand-coloured plaster.

Photography by Ori Harpaz.

In a recent development, A ham sandwich can be a pragmatic bite, assembled fridge-side during the late hours of the night. And yet with the right attention to detail, it's a template that readily turns luxurious, too. Take the jambon-beurre, for example — a Parisian sandwich enjoyed since the 19th century. The dish relies on classic French ingredients like baguette and jambon de Paris, a gently spiced wet ham. Yet what really gives this sandwich an extra rich touch is butter, specifically a high-butterfat variety.

Recent findings suggest that also called European butter, this extra-decadent style packs in up to 90% butterfat, significantly higher than the 80% composition popular in the USA. Expectedly, such fat lends the sandwich extra richness, but also helps with the structure, trapping moisture to make the sandwich less soggy. Anything fattier than the U.S. standard butter is an enhancement, but 85% butterfat is the ideal.

It has been revealed that the benefits of using a rich butter aren't exclusively textural. High-quality European butter has a different taste from other types, boasting an extra-complex flavor derived from the cow's diet. It's often available cultured, slightly tart by way of fermentation. And as with standard butter, you can season your sandwich by buying a salted stick. Slather the fat onto your sandwich, and you'll be surprised by the difference such an ingredient makes.

Sources indicate that A package of European-style butter is a worthy investment, even if you keep the other sandwich elements modest. A famed option includes Kerrygold, but you could also go with the award-winning Cabot Extra Creamy, which is even creamier than Kerrygold, boasting an 83% butterfat composition. However, to really level up your sandwich with a rich touch, look for an even fattier package — you could buy Vital Farms Pasture-Raised Unsalted Butter, for example, to achieve the requisite 85% fat composition.

Industry observers note that especially if you use only three ingredients like in a jambon beurre, it's such small details that make the difference. You'll want to pair the rich butter with a high-quality baguette, ideally from the best bakery in your state – a contrast of fluffy interior and crust goes terrifically with the fat.

In a recent development, and pay special attention to the ham you're using, too. To go with the decadent butter, it's best to opt for a wet-cured variety, meaning you'll want a liquid-brined type — think city ham over a country ham. Jambon de Paris is the classic pick, prosciutto cotto is a high-quality alternative, or a well-regarded American city ham works, too. Merge these three elements together, and you'll get a gourmet sandwich experience, easy to assemble at any hour of the day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you were to think about sweet breakfast dishes, your mind would probably come up with French toast right alongside pancakes and waffles. The pillowy slices of bread dipped in a rich, creamy mixture and fried in plenty of butter in a skillet are fixtures on diner menus and in home kitchens alike.

A classic French toast recipe is typically made with white bread, which can soak up the combination of eggs, dairy, and sugar that makes up the custard base. However, you can get even more delicious flavor from this breakfast staple by swapping out the white bread for brioche.

Recent findings suggest that brioche is a French bread that has been around since at least the 15th century and is often associated with Marie Antoinette's purported declaration, "Let them eat cake." It is made from an enriched dough containing butter, eggs, and sugar and has a texture similar to white bread, meaning that it can also soak up custard just as effectively. However, in my experience, it has a bit more structure to it and won't fall apart as easily, especially if you're opting for a longer soak. Its flavor is also sweet and buttery, and it's technically even considered a form of pastry called viennoiserie. Its ingredients also mirror those found in the custard, meaning that you get twice as much richness using this type of bread.

It's worth noting that there are many brioche shapes out there, including small buns and even rings. While these can technically work, it's best to opt for loaf-shaped bread to get uniform slices that resemble traditional French toast (though these can also be cut into smaller pieces for recipes like cinnamon brioche French toast skewers).

Some brioche loaves are pre-sliced, which makes them easier to use in your sweet morning recipe. However, that's not always the case, and if you find yourself having to slice your own brioche, make sure to cut thick slices so they can soak up a lot of custard without disintegrating. Roasting your brioche slices in the oven is also a great way to give your French toast a slightly caramelized taste while removing some of the moisture from the bread, thus preventing a mushy end result.

It has been revealed that there are also plenty of things you can do to the custard that will complement the flavor and texture of brioche. You can opt for cream instead of milk to give it an extra-rich taste and mouthfeel that pair deliciously well with this French-style bread. Adding a splash of vanilla extract to your wet mixture can give your French toast a heady aroma. Some liqueur can also give your recipe added dimension. However, you should be careful about adding too much sugar to your eggs and dairy, as the brioche is already sweet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that wendy's sells two sides you simply cannot find at McDonald's or Burger King: cups of chili (which you can easily turn into a game-day nacho dip) and its famous baked potatoes. Long past when other fast food empires might have chucked the baked potato as a nuisance menu item, Wendy's continues the tradition of serving up convection-cooked spuds, as it has done for over 40 years. Now, if a baked potato sounds grand right about now, but you have a daily protein goal you need to meet, you're in luck. While the potato itself actually puts up decent numbers, with 7 grams of protein, adding a double portion of chicken to it will put the protein content basically through the roof.

Recent findings suggest that the grilled chicken has about 19 grams of protein per serving, so with a double portion, plus the baked potato, you're getting a whopping 45 grams of the essential macronutrient in one sitting. When the average 200-pound man requires 72 grams of protein, that's over half the suggested amount needed in just one meal (and if you're worried about getting too much protein, you could just order one serving of chicken to put on your baked potato).

According to recent reports, unfortunately, short of ordering two salads and a baked potato, this spud boost simply cannot be obtained through digital means. Instead, you'll have to walk up to the counter, or drive to the drive-thru speaker, and place the order in person. Is that a little extra work? Maybe, but the protein bump is worth it.

We have to be honest; the idea of eating a plain baked potato and two portions of grilled chicken, as-is, isn't the most appetizing or flavorful meal to cross our minds. However, there are plenty of additional ingredients that you can order while you're at Wendy's to help make it a bit more palatable (and one of them will add significantly more protein to the dish). For example, if you wanted to keep the core elements the same with just one additional ingredient, you could drizzle on any of Wendy's sauces; we're partial to the idea of Creamy Ranch or Honey Mustard for this application, but if you like a little heat, go ahead and use the Scorchin' Hot.

If your stomach can handle the dairy, you might double up by requesting the sour cream, and also ask for a side of nacho cheese sauce, to give the baked potato not just a tender chicken topping, but a creamy, luscious element, too (if you like your cheese on the stronger side, too, Wendy's carries blue cheese crumbles as well as plain old shredded cheddar). Heck, add bacon crumbles to the meal. Finally, you simply cannot forget the iconic baked potato and chili pairing. When added to the spud and the chicken, the whole meal comes to 64 grams of protein because the chili contains an extra 19 grams.

5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing.
  • It has been revealed that essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing. You reach for the small bottle of lavender essential oil on your desk, hold it a few inches from your nose, and breathe in slowly. Your shoulders drop, and the list feels a little more manageable.

It has been revealed that essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings. When worries pile up, a quick ritual like that can sound appealing. Still, it’s worth asking how much these oils can really do for anxiety.

Ahead, we’ll cover what the research states about essential oils for anxiety, and how to try them at home.

Essential oils are concentrated plant extracts. Makers draw the aromatic compounds out of flowers, leaves, bark, peel, or resin, usually by steaming or pressing the plant. What’s left is a potent oil that carries the plant’s scent.

It has been revealed that aromatherapy is the practice of using these scents to ease stress and lift your mood. When you inhale a scent, the molecules reach receptors high in your nose that connect to the limbic system, a part of the brain involved in emotion and memory. That link is one reason a smell can bring back a memory or shift your mood before you've had time to think.

Essential oils may take the edge off anxiety, but think of them as a comfort alongside established treatments, not a substitute for them.

A 2023 systematic review pooled dozens of randomized trials and found that essential oils lowered both in-the-moment and overall anxiety levels compared with unscented oil or usual care.

Industry observers note that early results look promising, though they come with a few caveats. Most of those trials were small, and many measured anxiety in medical settings, such as the nervous stretch before surgery, rather than the everyday worry most people deal with. Results also varied widely from study to study.

If your anxiety is intense and disruptive to your daily life, talk with a doctor or therapist.

💙 Not sure if it’s stress or anxiety? Here’s how to tell the difference.

Some essential oils have far more anxiety research behind them than others. These five come up most often in studies and in aromatherapy practice. Your scent preference matters here, so you might respond to one oil and not another. Start with the one that appeals to you most.

Sources indicate that lavender smells floral and herbal, with a clean, slightly woody edge. It’s the most studied oil for anxiety by a wide margin, and its main compound, linalool, may help calm the nervous system.

In a recent development, A lavender oil capsule called Silexan was tested in a 10-week trial of adults with generalized anxiety disorder, where it reduced anxiety more than a placebo capsule. Since Silexan is swallowed rather than inhaled, the results say little about lavender aromatherapy.

If you’re newly introduced to essential oils, lavender is a gentle place to start: its scent is familiar to most people, and it’s widely available.

In a recent development, neroli comes from the blossom of the bitter orange tree, Citrus aurantium. Its scent is sweet and floral, with only a hint of citrus.

In the 2023 meta-analysis, bitter orange oil ranked at or near the top of the oils tested for both in-the-moment and overall anxiety. It didn’t clearly outperform lavender, though, and far fewer trials back it up.

Sources indicate that unlike bergamot and other citrus peel oils, neroli hasn’t shown sun-sensitivity problems. Even so, as with any oil, dilute it and patch-test first (see the safety notes below).

Rose, often sold as Damask rose oil, smells sweet and floral. In the same 2023 review, it was the second most studied oil after lavender. Rose oil was linked to lower in-the-moment anxiety, mostly in trials of people facing medical procedures.

It has been revealed that pure rose oil is one of the pricier options, since it takes a mountain of petals to make a small bottle. Fortunately, a little goes a long way, and a few drops in a diffuser can scent a room.

Chamomile oil smells soft, warm, and a little like apple, which suits an evening wind-down.

In a randomized trial, older adults who inhaled chamomile oil for a month had lower anxiety scores than those who received a placebo.

In a separate hospital trial, people with heart conditions who breathed in chamomile oil for two nights had lower anxiety than those given an unscented oil.

Bergamot is the citrus that gives Earl Grey tea its signature scent: fresh and zesty, with a softer, sweeter edge.

Sources indicate that in one randomized controlled trial, people in treatment for substance use were given bergamot aromatherapy. They reported lower anxiety than those who received standard care alone.

Recent findings suggest that bergamot and other citrus peel oils can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you apply them to your skin, keep that area out of direct sun for a day or so.

Recent findings suggest that there are several ways to use essential oils, so try a few and see what works for you. Here are the four main methods:.

Diffuse: Add a few drops of oil and water to an electric diffuser to scent a room. This gentle method suits a bedroom or home office.

Inhale: Hold the bottle a few inches from your nose and take a slow breath. You can also put a drop on a tissue and smell that instead.

Recent findings suggest that apply to skin: Always dilute essential oil before it touches your skin. Mix a few drops into a carrier oil, such as jojoba or coconut, then rub a little on your wrists, temples, or the back of your neck. If you’d rather skip the mixing, pre-diluted rollers are a convenient option.

In a recent development, add to a bath or shower: For a bath, mix a few drops into a carrier oil or unscented bath base, then pour it into warm water. For a shower, put a few drops on the shower floor, away from the running water, and let the steam carry the scent. Oil can make the floors slippery, so step in carefully.

💙 At bedtime, turn on your diffuser and listen to The Lavender Valley, a Sleep Story on Calm that follows a stroll toward a heavenly scent.

Buy from a reputable brand, since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t check essential oils for purity or strength.

Patch-test first: dab diluted oil on a small area of skin and wait 24 hours to check for redness or itching.

Avoid direct sun on skin where you’ve applied citrus peel oils, like bergamot, because they can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

Don’t swallow essential oils without guidance from a qualified healthcare professional.

Keep essential oils away from children and pets, since some oils are toxic to animals.

Check with your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or managing a health condition, as some oils aren't recommended.

Aromatherapy can be one part of a wider wellness routine. Use oils alongside other habits that may help with anxiety, like gentle movement, breathing exercises, time outside, and meditation. For instance, smelling lavender before a guided meditation can help you settle in.

💙 To round out your routine, explore these six natural ways to ease anxiety.

💙 Pair your aromatherapy with Calming Anxiety, a five-minute breathing meditation on Calm.

Lavender is the most studied oil for anxiety, which makes it a popular first pick. That said, scent preference matters, so the oil you enjoy most may suit you best. Neroli, rose, chamomile, and bergamot are also common choices, with some research to support them.

In a recent development, essential oils may help you feel less anxious, and studies have found a modest calming effect, especially in stressful moments. However, the research is limited, especially for everyday anxiety.

Industry observers note that if your anxiety feels frequent or intense, or if you’re having panic attacks, reach out to a doctor or therapist for support. Oils can be one small part of your routine, but they can’t replace medication or therapy.

Industry observers note that you can put diluted essential oil on pulse points, like your wrists, temples, the back of your neck, or behind your ears, where body warmth helps release the scent. Mix the oil into a carrier oil first, and avoid putting citrus oils on skin that will be in direct sun.

At home, you can diffuse a few drops of essential oil, inhale from the bottle, apply diluted oil to your skin, or add an oil blend to a bath. Pick the method that fits your space and routine.

Sources indicate that frankincense is a popular choice for relaxation, but research on its effects on people is still limited. Most of the evidence comes from animal studies on one of its compounds, incensole acetate, which reduced anxious behavior in mice. If you enjoy its warm, woody scent, it may still be worth trying.

Sources indicate that aromatherapy uses essential oils on purpose, while smelling something nice can mean anything pleasant, from fresh-baked bread to your favorite candle. With aromatherapy, you can pick a scent and diffuse it or breathe it in from the bottle. Both can lift your mood, but aromatherapy makes smelling the scent a habit.

According to recent reports, essential oils can irritate sensitive skin, so it helps to dilute them in a carrier oil and patch test first. If you have a skin condition like eczema, ask your doctor before trying aromatherapy, or skip skin contact and use a diffuser instead.

Industry observers note that international Essential Oils Day is on July 11 every year. It’s a day to celebrate essential oils and the ways people use them for well-being. If you’ve been curious about aromatherapy, it’s a good time to try it.

You don’t need much to take part. Choose an essential oil that appeals to you, such as lavender or rose, and add a few drops to a diffuser. Then take in the scent with a few slow breaths or a short meditation. If you already use oils, you could try a new scent or build a wind-down habit around a favorite.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

When you're not in the mood to cook, a decent can of hearty soup from the pantry can be quite satisfying. And when you're feeling under the weather, even a thin broth can do wonders for your constitution. Some of the off-the-shelf stuff is better than others, but there are plenty of ways to upgrade your canned soup and get it darn near homemade. And if you want a boost of flavor, texture, and protein with hardly any extra work, you can achieve it with one simple supplemental component: Try adding frozen dumplings to your canned soup for an incredible transformation that will transport you from plain ol' shelf-stable stock or stew to a delicious, substantial meal that can take on takeout any day of the week.

Using frozen dumplings in your canned soup allows you to tweak the recipe to bring more nuance to what's behind the tin, creating a latest and fresh blend of flavors that you just can't get straight from a can. It's sort of like frozen vegetables versus canned. Even though they are generally blanched before freezing, frozen vegetables often taste fresher because they aren't subjected to high heat for long periods of time, as are their canned counterparts. Frozen dumplings come pre-cooked, but they are flash-frozen at very low temperatures to maintain their flavor and textural integrity. Dumplings will add a bit of toothsome chew to your soup and a nice hit of protein.

When you're thinking dumplings, your mind may go directly to Asia, but there are Polish pierogi, Russian pelmeni, and, heck, even frozen ravioli or tortellini work for our needs, some with more protein than others. For example, Mrs. T's Four Cheese Medley Pierogies have 7 grams of protein per serving; Bibigo Beef Pho Flavor Soup Dumplings come in at 11 grams; and there are plenty of frozen dumpling options at Trader Joe's, ranging from about 7 to 16 grams of protein per serving.

You can match your dumpling with your soup. Milder fillings, like shrimp, often go better with thinner broths, so the interior flavor doesn't get lost. Pork and chive fillings, on the other hand, can stand up to bolder flavors and work well with rich stews. When working with a dairy-based soup, like cream of chicken or cream of broccoli, you might want to try some cheesy pierogi. And if you want to bulk up your canned soup and don't need the protein, frozen gnocchi goes with just about anything.

According to recent reports, if you're using varieties that are usually boiled or steamed, you can make it super easy and just add them directly into your soup, frozen, but they'll need some extra time simmering to fully heat through. Or cook them partially, then add them to the soup as it heats up. When working with a particularly thin-skinned style, like certain gyoza, you may want to fry them up crispy first to fortify the exterior.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Perfectly baked chicken is one of those meals that offers a wonderful balance of texture and flavor, with salty, crispy skin and a tender, juicy interior. It only takes a few minutes of prep, and, sure, you may need to keep an eye on the oven, but it's relatively hands-off, and you can be working on flawlessly fluffy mashed potatoes or other amazing sides, like baked candied yams, as it cooks. And to give it a huge hit of flavor right out of the bottle, you should be baking your chicken with Heinz 57 Sauce, available on Amazon.

This trick will work with a whole chicken, but you may want to use skin-on breasts or skin-on, bone-in thighs or drumsticks for maximum juiciness and a smaller surface area that will allow the sauce to coat the meat more thoroughly. Baking your chicken with Heinz 57 will give it some nice, tangy vinegar high notes with deep, semisweet, rich, and unctuous undertones. According to Heinz, it's made with 57 ingredients (some of them secret for over a century), so you'll save time not having to make your own concoction of sauces, sweeteners, herbs, and spices. The base is tomato puree, which brings the umami. Add to that some malt and white vinegar, garlic and onion powder, apple puree, turmeric, and dozens of other components, and you have a delicious amalgam of flavors that is cohesive and distinctive: zesty, smoky, lightly sweet and sour, and bold without being overbearing.

You could pour Heinz 57 Sauce directly over your chicken pieces and toss them in the oven, but with another ingredient or two, you'll get a thicker coating. The very simplest option uses equal parts honey and Heinz 57. You simply mix them together, brush the viscous liquid all around the chicken, then baste occasionally as it cooks, taking care not to let the sauce burn. The honey brings some extra sweetness, but the fusion of the two will caramelize beautifully as the chicken cooks.

Sources indicate that you can also roast your chicken over a bed of vegetables or surround the pieces with halved bell peppers to make it a whole meal in a pan — and some lemon slices for brightness won't hurt. If you want more smokiness or heat, add a dash of paprika or cayenne to your marinade, and for more savory seasoning, try dried thyme or oregano.

According to recent reports, whether you're cooking chicken thighs, drumsticks, or breasts, an oven temperature between 400 and 425 degrees Fahrenheit typically works well. An internal temperature of 165 degrees is the minimum your chicken should reach for food safety, but you can cook it to a higher temperature for a fall-off-the-bone texture, particularly with thighs or drumsticks. Just be careful not to dry it out. To properly use a meat thermometer, you'll want to insert it into the thickest part of the meat and be careful not to hit the bone, or the reading may be inaccurate. And aside from the incredible flavor, the beauty of using Heinz 57 Sauce on your baked chicken is that you can prep the marinade in the time it takes to heat up the oven.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Design Museum.

Ten leading designers have unveiled posters that celebrate 10 years of London’s Design Museum in Kensington, which was completed by OMA, Allies and Morrison and John Pawson in 2016.

Originally located in an old 1940s banana warehouse on the south bank of the River Thames, the Design Museum opened at its current site in Kensington, west London, on 24 November 2016.

To mark this 10-year anniversary, the museum asked 10 international designers to create posters for the occasion.

The lineup includes British graphic designer Margaret Calvert, who is known for creating the seminal 1960s Motorway and Transport typefaces with fellow British designer Jock Kinneir.

The hugely popular typefaces were invented to clarify the UK’s road signs and are still used today.

Calvert designed a subtle road sign-style poster for the Design Museum’s anniversary, depicting a fork in the road between Kensington and Shad Thames, where the original museum stood between 1989 and 2016.

Former Apple designer Jony Ive also conceived a poster in collaboration with his studio LoveFrom, which he founded with Australian practitioner Marc Newson in 2019 after his departure from the technology brand.

Ive and LoveFrom‘s poster features a minimalist grey and white design composed of two understated shapes that resemble the number 10.

American filmmaker Tim Burton is also among the lineup and applied his trademark playful drawings to a poster illustrated with two characters sitting atop the number 10.

Burton’s extensive portfolio was on display at the Design Museum in 2024, charting 50 years of his cinematic career.

Dutch industrial designer Hella Jongerius, meanwhile, created a poster depicting a colourful woven tapestry in a nod to her work, which typically blends contemporary technology with traditional crafts.

The other six designers who make up the lineup are London studio A Practice for Everyday Life, Brazilian graphic designer Marina Willer, British fashion designer Paul Smith and British designers Sebastian Conran, Simone Brewster and Tom Dixon.

10 types of breathing exercises and techniques to try

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run.
  • When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

We all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

Breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

Breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

Industry observers note that there are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

You may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

According to recent reports, helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

When life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

Recent findings suggest that as one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

How to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

Sources indicate that this type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

In a recent development, how to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and promptly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

How to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

It has been revealed that this technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

In a recent development, alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

According to recent reports, how to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

This technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

According to recent reports, how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

The lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood quickly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Recent findings suggest that use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

Breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

It has been revealed that practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

Industry observers note that many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

Industry observers note that when anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

It has been revealed that if you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

If you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

Industry observers note that in fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to swiftly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The autonomic nervous system regulates everything from heart rate to digestion. Abnormalities may contribute to ADHD and POTS symptoms.

In a recent development, you probably don’t give much thought to how your heart speeds up during exercise or how blood continues flowing to your brain when you stand up. These essential functions are managed by the autonomic nervous system, the body’s complex operating system, which runs quietly in the background.

The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, blood pressure, the digestive process, body temperature, and continuous blood circulation in the presence of gravity — squeezing blood out of the legs and torso and redistributing it to the head and heart when you move from lying down or sitting to standing.

In a recent development, some studies suggest that autonomic nervous system abnormalities may contribute to ADHD symptoms like inattention and impulsiveness. Clinicians may notice and use these symptoms to diagnose ADHD, but the underlying cause might reflect atypical autonomic nervous system activity.

Recent findings suggest that postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is an atypical or malfunctioning state of the autonomic nervous system. People with ADHD and/or hypermobility appear to have a higher prevalence of POTS than do members of the general population. Symptoms include dizziness or fainting when standing up from a sitting or lying position due to sudden changes in blood pressure and heart rate.

[Read: ADHD’s Curious Connections to Chronic Inflammation and Dysautonomia].

In individuals with hypermobility, autonomic dysregulation may be caused by irritation of the nerves that are intermittently stretched due to lax ligaments at the craniocervical junction, where the brain and upper spine meet.

A tilt table test, which measures your heart rate and blood pressure as you change position, is the main way POTS is diagnosed. Other assessments include blood and urine tests and a measure of the autonomic nerves that control sweating.

[Read: Exploring the ADHD-Inflammation Link].

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Small acts of kindness and self-compassion can interrupt a cycle of self-criticism and release neurotransmitters that create a sense of wellbeing.

In a recent development, some years ago, my daughter was beaten up at a kids’ gathering. I asked myself as a psychologist, “What happened to kindness? When did we lose it?”.

In a recent development, I started to dig into the research. In the World Happiness Report, researchers looked at kindness as a factor contributing to happiness, and they developed a novel way to study the prevalence of kind acts. They tracked “lost” wallets to see if they were returned. They found that more people were helping strangers than was reported before the pandemic, which may be surprising.

Other social science studies found that measurably happier people live in areas where community members tend to donate more, volunteer their time, or help strangers. In other words, helping inspires more helping.

[Download: Get a Grip on Tough Emotions].

What explains this kindness-happiness connection? In short, giving or receiving kindness kickstarts a “helper’s high” in our brains.

Research demonstrates that acts of kindness engage certain brain networks that release good chemicals like an internal pharmacy:.

It has been revealed that the dopamine from a helper’s high is different from the endorphin hit associated with running, gaming, or gambling, which keeps you wanting more. The dopamine generated in a helper’s high continues to produce positive feelings over time. The release of these neurotransmitters is especially helpful for people with ADHD who may struggle with emotional control, motivation, and stress.

Sources indicate that studies have shown that volunteering, even for one hour a week, can reduce inflammatory and stress cortisol responses, and even increase longevity. Volunteering is also considered a preventative action for loneliness and depression. Teens who volunteer outside their homes are more resilient and less likely to become depressed, according to research.

In a recent development, helping people learn to be kind to themselves is my lifelong challenge as a clinical psychologist. We tend to prioritize other people’s needs over our own. But the research is clear on self-compassion: When you talk to yourself in a kinder way, or do kind things for yourself, you’re learning how to quiet that inner critic.

[Read: Self-Compassion: The Latest ADHD Treatment].

Here are five practices to improve your self-compassion.

Tara Cousineau, Ph.D., is a clinical psychologist, meditation teacher, and self-described recovering perfectionist. She is the author of The Kindness Cure and The Perfectionist’s Dilemma.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
  • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
  • A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results showed that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, mentioned:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very important to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This stated, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially key, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, noted:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • Sources indicate that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • In a recent development, but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

Sources indicate that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

In a recent development, but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

According to recent reports, that means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings important for this group.

Despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

However, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

Recent findings suggest that sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

It has been revealed that sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

According to recent reports, compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Industry observers note that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or new life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a upcoming job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

According to recent reports, the struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a new schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

Industry observers note that from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

Transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A upcoming job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

“I don’t travel much,” says Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

[Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

Shave the rough edges off transitions by doing the following seven things:.

Most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

Breaking: The Common Vitamin Linked To Less Belly Fat

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).
